| `attachable/animation_controllers` | partial | An entry of `scripts.animate` naming a controller now runs it. Resolution is by short name against the attachable's own `animations` map, animations first and controllers second, so a controller naming another controller resolves to nothing - nothing in the surveyed corpus does it, and it needs a cycle check rather than an ordering. A controller the add-on does not ship resolves to nothing and plays nothing. Two of the three attachables in the corpus name `controller.animation.elytra.default`, which is in Mojang's resource pack; that file may not be vendored (constitution rule 10) and is not fetched at runtime. Its five states name animations those attachables mostly do not define, so most of it would draw nothing even if it were resolved. The machine's state is kept per holder, one transition per frame. SC-180 section 5.2. |

| `attachable/scripts` | partial | `pre_animation` runs first every frame, and its assignments are what the `animate` conditions read - evaluating them the other way round leaves every `v.` at zero, which answers "no" to every question a pack asks about itself. An `animate` entry's Molang expression is a BLEND AMOUNT, not a condition: SC-180 section 4.1.1. Every condition in the surveyed corpus is a comparison answering zero or one, so this is indistinguishable there and differs for vanilla's own entries, which blend a walk by `query.modified_move_speed`. An entry naming an animation CONTROLLER rather than an animation runs it - SC-180 section 5 - unless the controller is one the add-on does not ship, which is the case for the two attachables naming Mojang's `controller.animation.elytra.default`. An animation's clock is the HOLDER's, starting the first frame that entry's blend is non-zero and running from then on whatever the blend does. `scripts.initialize`, `scripts.scale` and `scripts.variables` are still not read. SC-180 section 4.1.1. |

| `attachable/first_person` | partial | It does need its own path, and the reason is not that hand rendering is awkward: Bedrock does not draw an attachable at the hand at all. It poses it in PLAYER space, which in first person is a space the game never draws in, because no player model is submitted. So the space is rebuilt against the camera - the camera's pitch and its yaw-over-body undone, the origin then dropped to the feet, and the whole scaled by the 0.9375 a player model carries. ORDER, not sign, is what that list is about. Stepping down to the feet before undoing the pitch drops the model along a tilted axis, misplacing it by 1.62 sin(pitch) horizontally - "looking up moves her up and forward, looking down the reverse". Pitch is undone because a player layer is not pitched either; Java tilts the head bone, not the body. Yaw is taken back to the BODY's, because Minecraft lets head and body differ by fifty degrees and a camera-anchored model slides off the player's back as the mouse moves. A worn attachable is not drawn in first person. The seam is the hand render, which is offered the two hands and nothing else; the four armour slots reach the third-person layer only. A halo sits above and behind the eye and would be invisible anyway, but an armour attachable that reaches in front of the player is a real omission rather than a hidden one. Confirmed against the Bedrock client in COMPOSITION: the body-parented character appears at the screen's left, point-blank, face visible, on both clients - the product of three measured rules (channels independent and translation outermost, SC-180 section 4.1.3; conditions fire, section 4.4; the wearer's `body` carries a half turn in first person, section 4.2.1), each read off original-content probes rather than fitted. The observable difference that remains: in first person the model sits slightly more centred and slightly nearer than the Bedrock client draws it - under a block, visible when the two screenshots are compared side by side, invisible without them. Both clients draw this pass with a fixed projection that ignores the FOV setting (measured), and the difference between those two fixed projections is not a vertical 60-versus-70: scaling camera-space x and y by tan(35)/tan(30) - the correction that premise derives - made the confirmed-matching character visibly worse. Five fitted constants and one derived one have died on this residual. No further constant goes in without a premise that survives the waist-parented character. |
| `attachable/worn` | partial | A worn attachable reaches the render layer only because the stack's minecraft:equippable names an equipment asset. Vanilla filters what it puts on the render state - HumanoidMobRenderer.getEquipmentIfRenderable asks HumanoidArmorLayer.shouldRender, which asks assetId().isPresent() - so a stack without one leaves headEquipment and its three neighbours empty and the layer is handed nothing at all. The asset named is ours and draws nothing: it declares a single layer of a type no humanoid renders, because the codec rejects an empty layer map and any type a humanoid DOES render would put a flat armour piece over the model. This lives on the STACK, so a stack made by an older build carries an equippable without the asset and stays invisible until it is made again (SC-120 section 5). That is a real upgrade hazard, not only a development one. Vanilla's CustomHeadLayer still draws the item's own flat model on the head, beside the attachable. Bedrock shows only the attachable. |
